台風が近づく前の九州から関東も油断は禁物です。日本列島には秋雨前線が延びていて、そこに向かって台風周辺の湿った空気が流れ込み、前線の活動が活発になる見込みです。すでに九州から関東にかけて雨が降っていますが、この24日(土)と25日(日)も雨が断続的に降るでしょう。大気の状態が不安定になり、雷雨や非常に激しい雨が降る所もありそうです。土砂災害や低い土地の浸水、河川の増水・氾濫に警戒が必要です。ただ、この土日の雨は降り続けているというわけではなく、止んでいる時間もあります。その間に側溝や雨どいの掃除、屋外にある飛ばされやすい物を片付けるなど、安全を確認したうえで台風の備えを行ってください。台風が接近する26日(月)～27日(火)は九州から関東は、さらに雨量が増え、大雨になる地点も増えるでしょう。台風の進路によっては大雨の地域や雨のピークの時間が変わるため、最新の情報を確認してください。

title: ウ南部停戦へ トランプ氏夫人仲介
body: Steve Holland　Ryan Patrick Jones[ワシントン／キーウ／モスクワ　２３日　ロイター] - 米ホワイトハウスは２３日、トランプ米大統領のメラニア夫人が、ロシア占領下にあるウクライナ南部ヘルソン州オレシュキでの停戦合意をロシアと‌ウクライナの間で取り付けたと発表した。停戦は２９日に開始する。ロシアとウクライナもオ⁠レシュキでの停戦合意を確認した。オレシュキは２０２２年２月からロシア占領下にあり、食料支援が滞るなどして住民の人道危機が深刻化。ホワイトハウスの声明によると、ロシアとウクライナは人道支援物資の​搬入と、指定された安全な回廊を通した民間人避難の準備を可能にするため、オレシュキでの全ての軍事行動を一時停止することで合意した。メラニア氏は声明で「オレシュ‌キの状況は極めて深刻だ。オレシュキは最前線の戦闘地域で、壊滅的な事態の瀬戸際にある。現地に残る住民の大半は高齢者で、医療支援や医薬品、食料、清潔な水を緊急に必要としている」とした。メラ‌ニア氏によると、停戦期間中はロシアとウク‌ライナ両国の非軍事チームが住民宅を訪問し、ロシアまたはウクライナ​への避難を希望する住民の移送を調整する。このプロセスを記録するために米国の報道機関が同行するとしたが、具体的にど‌の報道機関が同行するかは明らかにしなかった。＜ロシア、ウクライナ停戦合意確認＞ウクライナのアラハミヤ首席交渉官は、オレシュキでの停戦が近‌く実施されると確認。通信アプリ「テレグラ​ム」への投稿で、オレシュキと周辺地域からの避難と食料配送のために恒久的な‌人道回廊を設置する作戦を近く開始すると表明した。ただ、作戦の詳細は明らかにしなかった。ロシア大統領府のペスコフ報道官も、⁠米国の仲介でオレシュキを巡る局地的な停戦合意が成立したと確認。オレシュキからの退避を希望する全ての民間人に退避を認めるとし、避難には少なくとも数日かかるとの見通しを示した。オレシュキでの停戦についてはこのほど実施されたプ⁠ーチン大統領とトランプ米大統領の電話会談でも協議されていたと述べ、停​戦実現にメラニア氏が果たした‌役割を称賛。「人道作戦の調整に多大な貢献を果たしたメラニア夫人の尽力を歓迎する」と語った。ペスコフ氏の発表を受け、ロシア軍のゲラシモフ参謀総長はオレシュキでの人道作戦を円滑に実施するため、ロシア軍は現地時間２７日⁠午前４時（日本時間同日午前１０時）に攻撃を停止すると発表した。メラニア氏はこれまでも、戦時中にロシア⁠に連れ去られたウクライナの子どもたちを家族のもとに帰還させる取り組みに積極的に関与。声明によると、メラニア氏は代⁠理人とともに、局地的な停戦条件を取りまとめるためにロシアとウクライナ両国の指導部と直接協議を行った。オレシュキはドニプロ‌川を挟んでヘ⁠ルソン州の州都ヘルソン市の対岸に位置している。ホワイトハウスによると人口は高齢者を中心に​約１７００─２０００人と、ロシアによる全面侵攻前の約２万４０００人から減少した。同州のカホフカ水力発電所のダムが攻撃によって破壊された後、 オレシュキの約９０％が浸水したとされている。

title: パリ近郊で銃乱射 1人死亡4人負傷
body: [パリ ２３日 ロイター] - フランス当局によると、パリ西郊のトラッ‌プで２３日、男が車から発砲し、１人が死亡、１２歳の少⁠女を含む４人が負傷した。マクロン大統領はＸへの投稿で、「既に容疑者を拘束した​法執行機関に感謝したい。国家反テロ検察庁が本件を‌引き継いだ」と表明し、事件に深い悲しみを示した。トラップのアリ・‌ラベ町長はＢＦＭＴＶに対し、‌男が車から発砲し、「無差​別に発砲しているように見え、大量殺害‌を実行しようとしていた様子だった」と述べた。トラ‌ップに隣接す​るラベリエールのニコラ・ダン‌ビル町長は、容疑者について「近隣市プ⁠レジール在住の欧州系の人物」と説明した。ラベ町長は、犠牲者のうち２人がそれぞれア⁠フリカ系と北アフリカ​系だったと述‌べたが、他の犠牲者の背景についての詳細は明らかにしなかった。今回の銃撃は、２４─２５日の⁠抗議デモを控え、フランス国内⁠の緊張が高まる中で起きた。１７日には全国規模⁠の抗議デモが暴徒化した経緯がある。当局は、今回の‌銃撃⁠が人種や宗教を動機とするもの​だったのかについても捜査の対象に含めるとした。

title: 県立高で威圧的指導か 精神疾患に
body: 高校女子ハンドボールの強豪校として知られる茨城県立水海道二高で、女子ハンド部の男性コーチによる威圧的な指導で2年生部員1人が精神疾患を発症し、部活動に参加できなくなっていることが23日、関係者への取材で分かった。学校側は臨時保護者会で不適切な指導があったことを認めて謝罪し、コーチを指導停止とした。県教委も事態を把握し、当時の状況を確認するなどしている。関係者によると、2年生部員は9月中旬、部活動の練習中にプレーについて男性コーチの指導を受けた。練習後もコーチが持っていた傘の先を向けられ、至近距離で指導されたことで呼吸が荒くなり、別の部員に「手足がしびれる」と訴えた。帰宅後も症状が治まらずに救急搬送され、医療機関で「ストレスや緊張による過呼吸とみられる」との説明を受けた。この部員は後日、心療内科で精神疾患と診断され、現在も部活動に参加できない状態が続いている。学校側は同月に事態を把握。コーチへの聞き取り調査などから「不適切な指導と思われる案件があった」と認定し、コーチに指導停止を通告した。停止期間については、今後の調査結果などを踏まえて決定する。関係者によると、四位学校長は臨時保護者会でこれら一連の経緯を説明し、謝罪したという。四位校長は23日、茨城新聞の取材に「(不適切な指導と思われる案件について)重く受け止めている。生徒の安心安全につながる、正しい部活動の在り方を職員全体で求めていきたい」と語った。男性コーチは「管理職を通して(対応する)と言われている。申し訳ないが、ご理解いただきたい」と述べるにとどめた。同校は女子ハンドボールの強豪校。今夏の全国高校総合体育大会(インターハイ)は8強入りした。男性コーチは全国的に有名な指導者として知られ、年代別日本代表の監督を務めたこともある。現在は県ハンドボール協会の役員を務めている。

title: パナG従業員情報 外部AIにアップ
body: 大阪府門真市に本社があるパナソニックHDは、グループ会社で従業員と元従業員など約33万4000人の個人情報が外部に送出されていたときょう＝23日、明らかにしました。担当者が、会社で利用が禁じられている外部の生成AIに個人情報を含むデータをアップロードしたのが原因だとしています。発表によると、「パナソニックオペレーショナルエクセレンス」と子会社の「パナソニックデジタル」が共同で進める人事情報システムの導入プロジェクトで、担当者が2026年４月時点で人事情報システムに登録されていたデータの一部を、会社で利用が禁じられている生成AIにアップロードしたということです。対象となるのはパナソニックグループに在籍している従業員や元従業員とその家族で、具体的には●従業員・約７万5000人と、1978～2026年度に退職した元従業員：約17万8000人の社員番号、住所、電話番号、メールアドレス●従業員の家族が約５万5000人、元従業員の家族：約２万6000人（2016年以降退職の人のみ）で、従業員に代わる緊急連絡先の家族の氏名、住所、電話番号、メールアドレスが外部に送出されていたとしています。会社が生成AIの事業者に確認したところ、担当者がアップロードしたデータは「AI学習に利用する機能が無効となっていたので、ほかの利用者から関連する質問を受けても回答に使用されることはない」との回答を得たということです。こうしたことなどから、会社は「現時点で不正利用による具体的な被害は確認されておらず、今後二次利用されることはないことが確認できた」としています。会社は専用フォームのほか、問い合わせ窓口を設置していて「今回の事案を重く受け止め、個人情報の取り扱いルールおよび生成AIサービス利用管理の見直しを進めるとともに、関係者への教育・啓発を強化し、再発防止を徹底してまいります」とコメントしています。

title: 露 ウ南部で一時停戦合意と米発表
body: アメリカのホワイトハウスは23日、ロシアとウクライナがウクライナ南部の都市で一時的に停戦することで合意したと発表しました。トランプ大統領の妻、メラニア夫人が停戦を主導したとしています。ホワイトハウスによりますと、停戦の対象となるのはウクライナ南部ヘルソン州のオレシュキで、今月29日からすべての軍事行動を一時的に停止します。停戦は、人道支援物資の搬入や民間人の避難を目的としたもので、トランプ大統領の妻、メラニア夫人が主導したということです。メラニア夫人は、ロシアとウクライナの指導部と直接協議を進め、停戦の条件などについて合意を取り付けたとしています。オレシュキには現在、高齢者を中心に約1700人から2000人が残され、医薬品や食料、飲料水などが不足しているということです。

title: 高峰登山で不明2邦人か 遺体発見
body: 【バンコク共同】ネパール政府当局者は23日、ガンガプルナ西峰（標高7140メートル）で同日朝、2人の遺体を発見したと明らかにした。登山中の日本人男性2人が15日から行方不明になっており、当局者はこの2人の可能性があるとみている。当局はヘリコプターで遺体を収容する方針。2人を途中まで案内した山岳ガイドや当局によると、行方が分からないのは種石英典さん（40）と橋本哲さん（25）。ガイドは標高4900メートル地点まで共に登り、その後は付き添わなかった。15日に7050メートル地点まで到達したと連絡があったのを最後に所在が分からなくなり、19日から捜索が実施されていた。

title: ソウル市長 政治資金巡り逆転無罪
body:
【ソウル聯合ニュース】韓国のソウル高裁は23日、政治資金法違反の罪に問われた呉世勲（オ・セフン）ソウル市長に無罪を言い渡した。一審は罰金1000万ウォン（約118万円）の有罪だった。呉氏は2021年4月のソウル市長補欠選を前に政治ブローカーのミョン・テギュン氏に数回にわたり世論調査を依頼し、その費用を後援者に肩代わりさせたとして在宅起訴されていた。政治資金法違反では懲役刑や100万ウォン以上の罰金刑が確定すれば当選無効となる。

title: 滋賀銀と池田泉州HD 経営統合へ
body: 滋賀銀行と、池田泉州銀行（大阪市）を傘下に置く池田泉州ホールディングス（HD）が経営統合する方向で調整していることが23日、分かった。【ひと目でわかる】地銀グループの連結総資産顧客基盤の拡大を通じて、競争力を高める狙いがある。統合が実現すれば総資産は14兆円を超え、関西トップの地銀グループが誕生することになる。月内にも正式発表する。傘下銀行の合併は予定せず、持ち株会社を設立した上で統合する案を軸に検討を進めている。滋賀銀と池田泉州HDは同日、「経営統合を検討していることは事実」とのコメントをそれぞれ公表した。

title: 物価上昇2%到達判断の公算大 日銀
body: 日本銀行は、物価上昇率が目標の2%に事実上到達したとの見解を30日に初めて示す公算が大きい。今後の金融政策の重点が、物価の2%への「押し上げ」から2%の「定着」に転換する節目となる。日銀は政策金利の引き上げを今後も続ける方針だが、月内の利上げは見送る方向だ。【写真】金利の世界を徹底解説日銀は29、30日に開く金融政策決定会合で、一時的な要因を除いた「基調的な物価上昇率」が、物価安定目標の2%に達しているかどうかを議論する。結果は3カ月に1度改定する「経済・物価情勢の展望（展望リポート）」に書き込み、30日に公表する。展望リポートではこれまで、基調的な物価上昇率が「2026年度後半から27年度にかけて『物価安定の目標』とおおむね整合的な水準となり、その後も同程度で推移する」と見通してきた。

title: 佐川急便で情報流出 最大5323万件
body: 佐川急便は、「お荷物問い合わせサービス」が不正アクセスを受けた問題で、流出した可能性のある個人情報が最大でおよそ5323万件にのぼると発表しました。【写真で見る】スマート家電もサイバー攻撃の対象に?　ペット用の見守りカメラ乗っ取り…対象は、今年6月から9月までの送り状に記載された依頼主や届け先の氏名や住所などで、重複があるため実際の人数を示すものではないとしています。佐川急便は、セキュリティ対策と安全性の確認ができたとして、停止していたサービスをきょう再開しました。

title: パーク24 流出の146万人に見舞金
body: 不正アクセスを受け、運転免許証の画像を含む個人情報が流出したカーシェアリングサービス「タイムズカー」をめぐり、運営会社を傘下に置く「パーク24」は23日、被害者への対応などを発表した。本人確認画像の外部流出が確認された人に対して、お見舞金として3千円相当の現金または金券を渡す。お見舞金と今回の対応費用として特別損失55億円を2026年10月期決算に計上する。【画像】免許証画像が漏洩したらこんな懸念も発表によると、外部の専門機関によるフォレンジック調査を進めた結果、本人確認画像約146万4800件が外部へ送信された痕跡が確認されたという。これまでは、約160万件の流出の可能性があるとしていた。こうした顧客への対応として、「お見舞いとして3千円相当の現金または金券をお渡しする」としている。渡し方については現在検討中だという。今回の調査の結果、9月下旬の不正アクセスでは、退会者を含む662万8007件の個人情報が流出した。また、外部へ送信された痕跡は確認されなかったが、本人確認書類の画像へのアクセスがあったものも89万1602件確認された。

title: タイムズカー情報流出 集団訴訟へ
body: カーシェアリングサービス「タイムズカー」による情報漏えいの被害者側の弁護士は23日、サービスを展開する貸し駐車場大手「パーク24」側に集団訴訟を起こす意向を明らかにした。パーク24が示した運転免許証の画像データ流出に対する見舞金3000円が低額だとし、適正な金額の損害賠償を求めるとしている。【写真で見る】タイムズカーのユーザーに届いたメールの文面東京弁護士会所属の牧野裕貴弁護士は9月末に集団訴訟に向けた専用サイトを開設。23日時点で約9万人が登録したという。被害者からの正式な委任手続きを進める。提訴の時期や原告数は未定とした。牧野弁護士は「タイムズカー側は個人情報を適切に管理する義務を怠り精神的損害を与えた。2次被害防止の手間や、なりすましの危険性を考慮すると見舞金の金額は不十分だ」と述べた。パーク24は23日、氏名や住所、メールアドレス、運転免許情報など662万8007件の情報漏えいが確認されたとする調査結果を公表。運転免許証の画像データなど本人確認情報の漏えいが確認された約146万件については、画像データへのアクセスや外部送信を示す痕跡が確認された被害者に1人あたり3000円を支払う方針を示した。【安達恒太郎】

title: Deadly shooting near Paris is a 'racist terrorist attack', Macron says
summary: One person is killed and five wounded in a series of attacks. The suspected gunman has been apprehended.
body:
Watch: Emergency services at the scene of shooting near Paris
French President Emmanuel Macron has labelled a gun attack in a Parisian suburb which killed one person and injured five others "a racist terrorist attack".
Macron said the attack was a "turning point in the life of our Republic and our nation" - the first time there has ever been a random racial killing like this.
The attack unfolded over some 15 minutes with the attacker opening fire from his car - first in Trappes to the south-west of Paris, and then in nearby La Verrière - appearing to target people of migrant origin. He was subsequently arrested.
Three of those injured, including a 12-year-old girl, remain in a serious condition.
Visiting the scene of the attack in Trappes, Macron said people had been targeted for their skin colour or religion and urged the public not to give an inch in the face of what he called "ideologies taking root".
The exact motive remains unclear, but the National Anti-Terrorist Prosecutor's Office (PNAT) said the incident appeared to be "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise".
The suspect has been named in French media as Kevin T who, according to PNAT, had four previous convictions which had been "automatically expunged".
The 39-year-old was known to police but not to France's intelligence services, local media report.
He was not on a list of individuals considered to be a serious threat to French security, the national anti-terrorism prosecutor's office told BFMTV.
A member of the suspect's "immediate family circle" was also taken into custody on Friday, it added.
The Mayor of Trappes, Ali Rabeh, said that "an individual fired shots from his vehicle at several people he encountered" on Friday morning.
The gunman drove through several neighbourhoods in a grey Renault Clio, according to witnesses. Rabeh said he had  "fired randomly" with the seeming intent of causing "as many casualties as possible... he wanted to cause carnage", he said.
The mayor said people had been targeted at a petrol station, a medical centre and a playground in Trappes before the attacker had driven on to nearby La Verrière.
A police union official said the suspect had been detained in La Verrière on the main N10 road that runs through the town.
French police inspect the scene of the shooting in Trappes, near Paris
French firefighters and police were seen at a petrol station in the area
The mother of the injured 12-year-old told French broadcaster RTL her daughter suffered eight gunshot wounds and needed surgery.
"How could anyone do this to a child?" she asked.
The mother said her daughter had been wearing a headscarf and questioned whether this was why she was attacked.
"She's a child who was born in France, in Trappes. She has the right to live in France, to make her life in France," she added.
The attacker reportedly travelled down a main road, shooting intermittently out of his car window.
A local police chief told BFMTV that the suspect had used "an older-style semi-automatic weapon" with bursts of fire. Le Parisien reports that the gun dated back to World War Two.
PNAT said its investigation also includes "possession of a Category A weapon" - which includes military-grade weapons or weapons capable of firing in bursts.
The anti-terrorist office also said its investigation is looking into "conspiracy with a terrorist group for the purpose of preparing crimes against persons".
A big deployment of police and emergency services has been present at the scene

title: Seven shot dead by gunmen at church funeral in Jordan, officials say
summary: Thirty-four people are also injured in the attack in southern Karak governorate, and a manhunt is now under way.
body:
Watch: CCTV footage appears to show gunmen near church
Seven people have been killed in an attack on a funeral in central Jordan, officials have said.
At least 34 others were injured as gunmen opened fire on a church in Hmoud, in the Karak governorate on Friday.
The unidentified gunmen are reported to have arrived in a car, entered the church and opened fire before fleeing. No-one has admitted carrying out the attack.
In a news conference, Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said authorities were working to apprehend the perpetrators which he described as a "group of extremists".
Jordan's King Abdullah II said authorities would "confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties".
Initial reports indicated seven people had been killed in the attack. A government spokesperson later said six people had died, before officials again revised the death toll to seven.
CCTV footage, verified by the BBC, appears to shows three gunmen making their way from a road toward the church.
Two of the attackers are seen making their way on to what appears to be a vehicle entrance to the church grounds, before retreating briefly and returning with a third man. All three appear to be armed with handguns.
Separate footage believed to be from the aftermath of the attack appears to show several dead and wounded bodies on the ground amid chaotic scenes.
Between 150 and 200 people were in the church at the time of the shooting, according to one witness
Witnesses have described scenes of panic inside the church as people threw themselves under pews searching for cover, moving away from the windows.
Prayers and screams could be heard throughout the building as some tried to flee.
Khalid al-Mdanat was at the church and told BBC Arabic the attack lasted around 15 minutes with "people trying to flee while the shooting was still active".
"People began pushing and throwing themselves to the ground," he said.
"Some were taking cover, some were cradling the dead, others were holding their sons close, some were grabbing their children and fleeing, while others were holding onto their friends who were with them at the church."
He said the gunmen left through the church doors and fled in a pickup truck "firing as they went".
Another witness said: "I heard something as if a war had just started.
"I thought it was an electrical short circuit. I looked, people lying on the ground, wounded. The scene was catastrophic."
A woman in the church said explosions rang out seconds after a prayer.
"The sound of machine guns started, and the sound of glass. We began to realise that something was happening.
"People started screaming.
The witness described how the situation "continued to escalate for 10 continuous minutes". Once she ran out the church she said "bodies were all in the courtyards".
Al-Faraya has described the incident as "painful and horrific" and "unparalleled in the history of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan".
There was a heavy security presence at the entrance to a hospital treating people injured in the incident in Karak, amid an atmosphere charged with anger among residents of the governorate, particularly the families of those injured and killed.
Many looked distressed as roads were closed around the facility and people were forced to park their cars and continue on foot.
Security measures were also tightened ahead of the visit by King Abdullah II to check on the injured.
The atmosphere around the hospital remained tense as the sound of crying and shouting was heard as families mourned their loved ones.
Many people appear shocked, frightened and angry. Some expressed frustration at what they described as "a failure to take a tougher approach towards terrorists".
Karak has a sizeable Christian community in the majority-Muslim Jordan.
Such violence is rare in the country, but deadly attacks have been carried out in the past.
Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun, a Christian head of state, said the "heinous terrorist attack" on the church "violated the sanctity of death and funeral mourners, contradicts all religious and humanitarian values," according to Lebanese media.
Additional reporting by Majdi Gousous, BBC Arabic.

title: Freed US citizen was tortured in Russian jail, former Ukrainian prisoners say
summary: Ukrainians held alongside the American say they witnessed beatings and sexual humiliation by Russian guards during his detention.
body:
Stephen Hubbard (second from left in the first row) was flown back home on a US plane earlier this week
Ukrainians held alongside freed US prisoner Stephen Hubbard have said they witnessed him being beaten and humiliated by Russian guards during his four-year detention.
Dmytro Khyliuk first met Hubbard at the Novozybkov prison in Bryansk, not far from Russia's border with Ukraine, in September 2022.
"We heard it from the guards. They came during inspections and were asking: in which cell is the American? And then they used obscene words. They threatened him, they mocked him from the first days."
Ihor Shyshko also remembers Hubbard's arrival at the jail and says his nationality marked him out to the officers.
"It attracted such attention because they mocked him, forced him to learn the Russian language, sing the national anthem and repeat the rules of the prison schedule, which he could not read."
Hubbard was captured in April 2022, when Russian soldiers occupied the eastern city of Izyum, where he was living with his Ukrainian partner.
He was accused of serving in Ukraine's armed forces and convicted in a trial in Moscow before being sentenced to six years and 10 months. Shyshko and Khyliuk were held alongside Hubbard as he awaited trial.
Ihor Shyshko alleges that Hubbard was subjected to sexual humiliation and abuse for the entertainment of Russian prison staff
Shyshko said he witnessed and heard Hubbard being beaten by prison guards and electrocuted with a stun gun.
"They beat him on the legs, on the back, on the arms," he said. "Of course, they didn't give him food, they didn't give him medical care. They kept him in the cold.
"He was always treated more harshly, because he was an American. They claimed he was a mercenary, and said 'let's beat him'."
Shyshko, a captured Ukrainian soldier, alleges Hubbard was subjected to sexual humiliation and abuse for the entertainment of the prison staff.
Accounts from the two former Ukrainian prisoners corroborate statements made by Hubbard's family that he was tortured in prison.
The 74-year-old was released by the Kremlin after four-and-a-half years, on the day US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg to discuss the war in Ukraine.
Witkoff praised the Russian President as a "humanitarian", despite the ongoing full-scale invasion and daily Russian attacks across Ukraine.
US President Donald Trump said he had asked Putin to free Hubbard during a phone call the week before.
Dmytro Khyliuk says Hubbard was hidden in a Russian prison to conceal his condition from a team of International Red Cross visitors
Khyliuk, a journalist, was held in the earliest days of the invasion, when Russian troops advanced towards the capitalKyiv.
He said he knew Hubbard's health was declining over the months they were initially held in nearby cells because he heard his complaints and the guards calling him more often to see the prison doctor.
Khyliuk described broken windows and biting cold, with detainees using time out of their cells to huddle together in the bathroom for warmth.
"It was very difficult conditions in Novozybkov, worse than in the next prison. It was very cold there in winter, terribly cold," he said.
Both men encountered the retired English teacher again at their next prison, Pakino, where Shyshko says Hubbard's condition worsened.
"There was not a single spot on his knees or on his feet without rot," he said.
"Everything was rotten. We all had scabies. It was very, very difficult for him. I even bandaged him once at the medical centre, because the doctor didn't want to do it. He just couldn't do it himself, and I had to help. He was quite weak then and he almost couldn't move."
They detailed a harsh regime and a meagre diet of porridge, bread and potatoes, with a daily routine of beatings and humiliation, being forced to run or hold stress positions.
"There's a handler with a dog, who lets go so it can bite you on the buttocks, on the elbow, or bite your leg. Then these wounds fester very badly," Shyshko said.
Khyliuk claimed that soon after their transfer to Pakino, Hubbard was hidden to conceal his condition from a team of International Red Cross visitors.
"I would like to say that an international humanitarian organisation that receives a lot of funding could do better. They saw only what was shown to them and they were happy with that," he said.
The International Committee of the Red Cross said in a statement that "in any situation where the ICRC has been granted access, we request to see every individual and assess the conditions they are held in. We continue our discussions with parties to the conflict on this issue."
Khyliuk said Hubbard disappeared from the prison in 2024 and he thought he must have been released. Khyliuk was returned to Ukraine in August 2025 in a prisoner exchange.
He likened their treatment to the regime of Soviet leader Joseph Stalin.
"Russian captivity is a torture machine. From the first second of your detention, they do everything to suppress you, to intimidate you. This is torture in all its manifestations, from psychological to physical. Beatings, hunger, cold, lack of any information, lack of the opportunity to communicate even with other prisoners".
Khyliuk said he was pleased to see Hubbard finally released and heading to the US.
"I understand what it is like to be in terrible captivity. Moreover, it was not his war. He ended up in the wrong place and at the wrong time," he said.
But he described the timing as "shameful PR of the US president, who is losing votes in elections to Congress".
Shyshko said he hoped one day their torturers would face justice.
"Evil must be punished, and so it will be. I have hope for that".
Hubbard was sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony in 2024, accused of serving in a defence unit in eastern Ukraine

title: Israeli forces begin demolishing Palestinian buildings in Hebron after two Israeli soldiers shot dead
summary: The soldiers were killed in an attack by two Palestinian gunmen at a checkpoint outside the West Bank city on Friday morning.
body:
Diggers were seen demolishing Palestinian homes on Friday afternoon
The Israeli military has begun demolishing Palestinian buildings in the city of Hebron, after two Israeli soldiers were killed in an attack by two Palestinian gunmen.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the military would "destroy" the neighbourhood where the two attackers came from, and that Israel was ready for "extensive action" in the occupied West Bank.
Three other soldiers were wounded in the attack at a checkpoint outside Hebron, before the gunmen were shot dead, officials say.
It comes at a time of high tensions, with extremist Jewish settlers targeting Palestinians during the annual olive harvest, and Israel's general election taking place in four days' time.
Footage verified by the BBC shows an intense gun battle between soldiers and the gunmen. Other footage shows two gunmen exit a car armed with what appears to be a handgun and an assault rifle and start firing on soldiers at the checkpoint, before coming under return fire.
Photos of one of the suspected attackers were shared by AFP news agency
The incident has already begun to influence the ongoing election campaign, with Netanyahu - who has built his campaign on the promise of security - saying that his Likud party would cancel campaign events which had been set for Friday morning.
Speaking later from the scene, Netanyahu said that the military would "demolish this place and completely transform it," referring to the Hebron neighbourhood where the attackers are said to have come from.
It is common for Israeli forces to demolish the homes of Palestinians who are suspected of carrying out attacks on Israelis -a practice Israeli rights groups have criticised as collective punishment.
Netanyahu likened his plans to previous operations in West Bank refugee camps where residential buildings were demolished and thousands were displaced.
He also said he had reviewed plans for the largest military operation in the West Bank in decades - though did not say when it could be carried out.
He added that he had imposed cordons around the city of Hebron - which has around 200,000 residents - and the nearby city of Halhul.
Netanyahu's far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for Israel to launch a campaign in the West Bank "exactly like in Gaza or Lebanon," while far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir called for Israel to dismantle the Palestinian Authority.
On Thursday, Foreign Minister Israel Katz accused opposition leaders of undermining the government by criticising Netanyahu's warnings of an attack ahead of the election, saying they would be "responsible" for any future attack on the country.
Opposition chiefs, including frontrunner Gadi Eisenkot and former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, offered their condolences to the families of the killed troops and praised those who killed the attackers.
The Israeli military said it had found a large quantity of ammunition in the attackers' vehicle, and that they believe the gunmen had intended to carry out a much larger attack on the nearby Route 35, but ran into the checkpoint - so instead decided to open fire there.
At least 96 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank since the start of the year, according to the UN.
Four Israelis, both security forces and civilians, have been killed by Palestinians there over the same period, the UN says -not including those killed in Friday's attack.

title: White House says Melania Trump brokered truce for Ukraine city 'on brink of disaster'
summary: Ukraine and Russia confirm the truce in Russian-occupied Oleshky, where residents have had to eat garden weeds to survive.
body:
These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this year
US First Lady Melania Trump has "successfully secured" a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, the White House has said.
It said the truce in the "front-line war city on the brink of disaster" without medicine, food and clean water would begin on 29 October.
Ukraine and Russia confirmed the deal was agreed to evacuate residents and deliver aid. They both said their forces would stop firing at 02:00 GMT on 27 October.
Oleshky was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Trapped between Ukrainian positions across the Dnipro River and Russian forces to the east, residents have recently resorted to eating garden weeds to survive.
Trump: First lady's 'initiative' led to truce for Ukraine city
The White House statement said Melania Trump and one of her representatives had worked "directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localised ceasefire".
"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," she is quoted as saying.
"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive co-ordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine."
Melania Trump added that Oleshky residents "have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks" and that "without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible".
The statement did not say how long the ceasefire would be in place for.
Davyd Arakhamia, a Ukrainian MP who heads President Volodymyr Zelensky's party in parliament, later said "an operation to unblock the settlement of Oleshky and its surroundings will begin in the near future".
"To achieve this goal, a ceasefire will be achieved in the near future, as announced by the First Lady of the United States, Melania Trump," he said.
In Russia, President Vladimir Putin's spokesman confirmed that, "those who wish to do so will be able to leave this settlement".
Oleshky has been without gas or electricity since 2023, so residents have had to find other solutions
Last month, some of the remaining Oleshky residents told the BBC harrowing accounts of how they were surviving in the city that was being constantly shelled and cut off from food and water.
They said that children remaining in wider Oleshky were suffering from malnutrition, a lack of medical services and were "degrading" without access to education.
Many also told the BBC there was only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations.
The local population was living under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, according to Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha.
Ukraine says it has attempted to deliver supplies to the area but has not had success in recent months.
The Kremlin in September acknowledged that Oleshky was facing "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv.
Oleshky was home to 24,000 people before Russia's full-scale invasion. Now  Ukraine estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children.
It is also one of a number of settlements where thousands of people lost their homes to a massive flooding caused by the collapse of Nova Khakovka Dam in 2023. Ukraine and its allies accused Russia of blowing up the dam, while Russia blamed Ukraine.
Melania Trump worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to agree the ceasefire, the White House said.
While the US first lady is relatively lower profile than some of her predecessors - and only occasionally seen at White House events - she has become involved in addressing humanitarian issues stemming from the Russia-Ukraine war.
In August 2025, Melania Trump penned a letter to Putin, telling him it was "time to protect children and future generations worldwide".
Although she did not mention Ukraine by name, just days later at the White House Zelensky handed over a letter from his wife Olena, thanking her for her efforts on children.
In a rare public appearance in October the same year, the US first lady said that Putin had answered directly in writing and that her representatives were working with the Russian president's team to repatriate Ukrainian children from Russia and vice versa.
Some 34 children have reportedly been returned since 2025, including five this July.
According to US President Donald Trump, his wife has also privately expressed scepticism about Putin and his desire to achieve peace.
"I'd get home, I'd say, 'First lady, I had the most wonderful talk with Vladimir. I think we're finished'," Trump said in July last year.
"And then I'll turn on the television, or she'll say to me one time, 'Wow, that's strange because they just bombed a nursing home.'"

title: Civil servant who juggled five jobs says he was 'surprised' to be charged with fraud
summary: Kashim Chowdhury denied being dishonest when not telling employers he had other jobs.
body:
Civil servant Kashim Chowdhury is accused of fraududlently earning more than £284,000 by juggling multiple public sector jobs.
A civil servant accused of fraudulently juggling multiple government jobs says he was ''surprised'' to have been charged with fraud.
Kashim Chowdhury told the jury at Southwark Crown Court he had not been dishonest in failing to tell his employers he had other government jobs.
"At that time I was just on auto pilot, I was like a robot, I was not thinking clearly," he said.
Chowdhury, 55, from east London, is accused of nine counts of fraud. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain.
Between 2020 and 2023 Chowdhury had eight overlapping public sector jobs. He was contractually obliged to work full time and was paid a full-time salary by each organisation. He is accused of fraudulently earning more than £284,000.
In March 2023 Chowdhury began working for the Home Office despite being under contract to work full time at the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), the Department for Business and Trade and the Food Standards Agency.
The court was told he started the Home Office job while on sick leave from three of his other jobs.
Prosecuting barrister Lucy Organ asked him: "If you were really sick for work, how were you able to start your work at the Home Office?"
Chowdhury  said: "I did not want this job at the Home Office, I was told there would be adequate support and I could work whatever hours I wanted to work."
Organ also asked why he did not submit a sick note to the Home Office "You were using these sick notes to be able to cope. It was all too much wasn't it?"
Chowdhury rejected the suggestion, adding: "I wanted to carry on working."
In May 2023, Chowdhury was contracted to work 183 hours a week, more than the number of hours in seven days.
He told the jury he agreed with his employers to work flexibly and that his work was project or output based. He said this was agreed "informally" via text messages but the phones used to send the texts had gone missing when his house was searched by investigators.
He said that to cope with the workload he would work from 07:00 on Saturdays and Sundays and not finish until 20:00 or 21:00.
Civil servant faked illness with make-up to juggle five jobs, court hears
Civil servant admits he 'made mistakes' juggling five government jobs
Organ asked him: "Wasn't that a bit much for you?"
"I was house bound, I was looking after my mum," he said.
The prosecution alleges Chowdhury managed to keep his overlapping jobs secret because he worked entirely remotely. He told his employers he was the sole carer for his elderly mother and the prosecution alleges he "exploited this opportunity".
His line manager at the UKHSA, Aleesha Adams, organised a video call with him in May 2023 to discuss his sick leave.
She previously told the court she was surprised when he logged on wearing white make-up because his name led her to expect to see an Asian man with darker skin.
She told the court that as the meeting went on the make-up started coming off his forehead. ''He was sweating, it was like rubbing off so it was darker underneath and darker on the neck."
But Chowdhury denied having worn make-up at the meeting
''That's a smear, I've never worn make-up in my life. At that particular time, I was suffering from anxiety and depression. I had already submitted my sick note, there was no need to put on make-up.''

title: White House lifts tariffs on some Canadian goods as midterm elections loom
summary: From 30 October, tariffs will be eased on some products, including certain machinery, and placed on others, such as carpets.
body:
Canada and the US are currently locked in a tit-for-tat trade war
The Trump administration is lifting some of its 50% tariffs on Canadian goods two weeks before the midterm elections, after a Republican candidate in a key Senate race said she had lobbied for the change.
Starting on 30 October, tariffs will be eased on products including "plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment," the White House said on Friday.
Republican Senator Susan Collins, who is in a tight race to keep her seat in Maine, first announced the exemptions, saying they would help her state's agriculture industry.
The US imposed a 50% levy on $20bn (£15bn) of Canadian goods after trade talks between the two countries collapsed in August.
Maine Senator Susan Collins is seeking to keep her seat in November's midterm elections
Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures against US tariffs, which Prime Minister Mark Carney said were "necessary to protect our workers".
Last month, Carneymatched the US tariffs"dollar for dollar" after the breakdown in talks. Trump had imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US cars, dairy and alcohol.
The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts
The White House said while tariffs would be lifted from some items, including some packing crates and boxes, they would be introduced on other items such as carpets and "waste products".
It said the action reflected President Trump's "continued efforts to defend American workers and ensure fair trade".
In a statement to the BBC, Canada's internal trade minister Dominic LeBlanc said: "While we assess these latest steps, Canada stands ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada's interests."
The White House's announcement comes less than a fortnight before the US midterm elections, which will determine whether Trump's Republican Party or Democrats will control Congress, impacting the remaining two years of his term.
Collins said she had repeatedly asked senior Trump officials for tariff relief and that she would "continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbour, ally, and largest trading partner".
She wrote on X that the tariff exemptions were on products that were "crucial to Maine's agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers".
Collins' Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, responded: "Trump's trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers. Susan Collins enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it, and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire."
Maine borders the Canadian provinces New Brunswick and Quebec. Its economy, as well as that of other border states, is deeply linked to Canada and they have felt the effects of the months-long trade war.
Michigan lawmaker Mike Rogers, also a Republican, has called on Trump to end the standoff after spending months supporting the policy in recent advertisements airing in his trade-reliant state.
Also on Friday, President Donald Trump said Canada was "working very hard" on a ⁠trade ​deal with the US.
Carney, for his part, said that Canada was open to a mutually beneficial deal, but is willing to wait it out.
"We could sign it this afternoon if the US were there. If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration, before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that," he said on Friday, according to Canadian broadcaster CBC.
LeBlanc confirmed on Thursday that a delegation met with members of the Canada-United States Economic Relations Advisory Committee - the ninth meeting since April 2026. The committee members discussed the ongoing impact of US tariffs in Canada.

title: Earnings limit of up to £140K for first-time buyers loan scheme
summary: The Your First Home scheme will offer government-backed loans for those buying new-builds in England.
body:
Households will need to earn less than £110,000 to qualify for the government's new loan scheme for first-time buyers, or £140,000 for homes bought in London.
Asfirst reported by The Times,external, the earnings limits are expected to be confirmed at the Budget next week.
The Your First Home scheme will offer government-backed equity loans worth 20% of new-build properties in England bought from participating developers.
The loans, which will also be subject to an initial interest-free period, are designed to help people buy a home with deposits as low as 2.5%.
Previous schemes to help first-time buyers did not restrict eligibility by income but faced criticism for stoking house prices by allowing relatively wealthy households to borrow more.
Unveiling the Your First Home Scheme at last month's Labour conference, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it would focus on those who "really need support".
The Times reported that ministers had initially decided to set the earnings limits at £90,000 for homes outside outside London and £110,000 in the capital, before concluding this would deny access to too many middle-earning couples, such as teachers and nurses.
The government has also argued that the scheme will help to boost housebuilding, after ministers conceded they areset to miss a targetto build 1.5 million homes in England by the next election.
Labour has said the scheme will be funded by within existing government budgets, but is yet to provide details of which other areas will see their spending cut.
Developers taking part in the scheme will also be asked to contribute towards running costs.
The Home Builders Federation, which represents developers, has welcomed  the plans and urged the government to move quickly to set up the scheme.
The Conservatives have however branded the proposals a "colossal admission of failure" of Labour's housebuilding record, and expressed concerns that the new developer levy could push up the price of new homes.
Like the Help to Buy scheme launched under the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government, the scheme will use equity loans, which are linked to changes in the value of properties they are used to purchase.
That scheme, which initially ran between 2013 and 2021, enabled all home purchasers to put down a 5% deposit on a newly built home worth up to £600,000.
Up to 20% of the cost of the home was funded by a shared equity loan, which was interest-free for the first five years.
A second version of that scheme, which ran from 2021 to 2023, restricted access to first-time buyers and applied regional-level price caps to the properties could be bought under the programme.

title: Lights will stay on this winter, grid operator says after concerns
summary: The assurance from the National Energy System Operator comes amid concern from its engineers about their ability to ensure adequate supply.
body:
The lights will stay on this winter, the body in charge of Britain's electricity network has said after concerns were raised by some of its engineers.
The National Energy System Operator (NESO) said the country's electricity system was prepared and "resilient to the challenges it may face" during the colder months.
However, its winter outlook report comes after an independent investigation found engineers had "high levels of stress and concern" about their ability to ensure adequate supply due to differences between renewable and gas-fired power generation.
NESO said supplies were expected to remain secure throughout the winter, though warned there could be "tight days".
It added that such days would result in it deploying notices to power producers that additional electricity generation may be needed. It said such an announcement was not a warning of power cuts and was routine.
"While we never take resilience for granted, households and businesses can be confident that Great Britain's electricity system remains secure, reliable and among the most resilient in the world," said Deborah Petterson, director of whole energy system resilience at NESO.
In a separate report, National Gas, a private company that owns and runs the country's gas network, and is separate from NESO, said it expected to have sufficient supply to meet demand this winter, but forecast gas for power generation to increase at peak demand due to the "intermittent" nature of renewables.
The release of the two reports comes as Britain's energy generation and security falls under increasing scrutiny, given the wars in the Middle East and eastern Europe have pushed prices up and sparked supply fears.
The country's electricity is generated from a wide range of sources, including renewables such as solar and wind, as well as more traditional gas-fired and nuclear power stations.
Wind power was the largest generator of electricity in Britain last year, accounting for almost 30% of all power, marginally above gas.
However, there appear to be challenges in the transition to renewables in ensuring supply keeps up with demand, according to findings from an investigation into practices at NESO, which was commissioned following allegations over operational decision making and record keeping at the grid operator.
Law firm Eversheds Sutherland, which carried out the independent investigation, said there were "high levels of stress and concern" within NESO's Electricity National Control Centre over the "current state of the energy industry generally" and the longer-term ability to keep it balanced.
It said this was, according to evidence gathered from staff, due to the fact that traditional methods of electricity generation such as gas were "easier to manage", compared to renewables, which were "less flexible", and were making the job of ensuring supply meets demand "more difficult".
The probe also found there to be a "significant disconnect" between those working in the control room and NESO's leadership.
Multiple witnesses expressed the view that those in senior leadership and executive positions "do not fully appreciate or understand either the way in which the control room works, or the reality of the pressures faced by those on the frontline who are responsible for 'keeping the lights on'", Eversheds' report said.
The investigation was prompted after Conservative shadow energy secretary Clare Coutinho said in July she had been contacted by a whistle-blower alleging that NESO had been "hiding information about how securely our grid is being run".
One of the claims was that control room staff were encouraged to conceal or alter records to avoid leaving a paper trail linked to efforts to stabilise the grid during a period of extreme heat in June.
This was done in order for NESO, which is owned by the government, to avoid public scrutiny or reputational damage, according to the allegation.
Eversheds said its investigation did not substantiate any of the allegations from whistle-blowers but did identify "cultural, governance and control issues" that it said were "significant findings in their own right".
Fintan Slye, chief executive of NESO, said the investigation identified "areas where we could improve how colleagues can raise concerns and how we respond to them".
"I want all colleagues at NESO to feel heard. We will act on the recommendations, working closely with our trade unions, and be open with colleagues about the progress we make," he added.

title: 'I'm 96 and have 15 million followers': The grannies taking over TikTok
summary: Grandma Droniak, Nonna Gracie, Viv Truran and Barbara Costello have all found fame on social media in their later years.
body:
Grandma Droniak pays for her care home fees with the money she makes from brand deals on social media
Ninety-six-year-old Lillian Droniak, known as Grandma Droniak to her social media followers, went viral in June after claiming her retirement home had threatened to evict her for throwing parties.
The home later confirmed the threat, but reached a settlement with Droniak that  allowed her to keep partying – but not supply alcoholic drinks.
With 15 million followers, Droniak has turned her personality into a lucrative business, earning enough from social media to cover her nursing home fees of $12,000 (£9,000) a month.
The Connecticut grandma is one of many older women finding unexpected fame online, with most of their audiences often young enough to be their grandchildren.
From fashion and food to dating and homemaking, they are finding new audiences and, in some cases, a new lease of life.
Watch: Nonna Gracie on what she wants the younger generation to know
"I always knew I had it in me to be famous, I just didn't think it would happen in my 90s," Droniak tells me, explaining that her grandson began helping her post videos in 2020, initially out of boredom.
She believes her appeal lies in showing younger people that life doesn't stop as you get older.
"They think old people just sit and stare at a wall but I'm showing it's not that bad to get old. We embrace it, can still have fun and I'm still partying and going out sometimes."
Her grandson edits her sponsored content, which includes partnerships with food and beauty brands. As well as paying for her nursing home fees, the money also goes towards a college fund for her great-grandchildren.
Despite being recognised by fans in public, she says her fame feels different at the retirement home. "They don't get it as they don't go on TikTok."
On the other side of the Atlantic, there's Viv Truran, an equally cheeky and cheery 82-year-old from Cardiff.
She started posting on Instagram after losing her husband and her neighbour suggested filming her colourful outfits.
Viv Truran shares her colourful outfits with her more than 800,000 followers
Now she makes two videos a day from her bedroom-turned-studio, showing off her clothes, 22 pairs of glasses and two drawers of scarves.
"I get up in the morning, I never come downstairs until I've done my morning video and I'm very strict about that."
She also keeps a notebook tracking her followers and views – and is now on book five.
Truran is regularly stopped by strangers, many of them women in their 20s and 30s, who tell her they are "frightened of getting old" and she shows them "it's not that bad".
Brands have taken notice too and Truran says she'd "be stupid" not to do deals but is selective.
She does a couple of sponsored posts a month, prioritising local brands and charities such as Age UK. She recently worked on an Age UK campaign in partnership with Innocent Drinks, which paid her several thousand for the collaboration.
"I've turned down some big deals because it's not my thing. I'm very picky about who I work with, I have to really love the brand."
Naomi Barker from influencer marketing agency We Are Social says older creators are attractive to brands as they often have "deeply established, highly loyal" communities with greater purchasing power, which "carries a massive premium".
Nonna Gracie has been dubbed "the internet's Italian grandma"
Grace Geramita, 83, has millions of followers who watch her cook recipes she has made for decades.
Known as Nonna Gracie, she moved from Italy to the US when she was 18 and worked multiple jobs at once to provide for her two daughters. Now, she earns more than she ever made in a previous job.
Her grandson Matthew suggested they start filming her cooking six years ago but Geramita wasn't keen as she knew nothing about social media and doesn't "speak very good English", but the videos took off.
"I always cry when people send me messages from all around the world," she says.
Much of her content is about more than food – she says she wants to pass on the "tradition of bringing family together around the table".
Barker from We Are Social says this is part of the appeal of TikTok grannies as they "offer comfort in an uncertain world".
Their wholesome content can also act as a "virtual grandma" for followers, she says.
Barbara Costello says many people see her as the mother or grandmother they never had
That's certainly the case for Barbara Costello. The 77-year-old former teacher now shares videos about cooking, cleaning and homemaking skills on her Brunch with Babs accounts.
Her followers tell her she reminds them of their own mothers and grandmothers, with some calling her "the mom I never had".
"Recently, a university student approached me in a restaurant to tell me my cookbook had helped her through her first year living independently and I was so happy."
Costello works with brands but says she has to think carefully about if it's something she wants to put her name on.
She says the best part of being a creator is seeing former pupils at her book signings with their own children.
"It's a full circle moment. I really can't believe this is my life."

title: Burnham suggests stocking up on tinned food and bottled water
summary: The prime ministers says unexpected events seem to be becoming more common and it was wise to prepare.
body:
'Be prepared': PM Andy Burnham suggests stocking up on basic food items
The prime minister has advised people to stock up on tinned food and bottled water in order to be prepared for emergencies.
With storms battering the UK, and in the wake of online disruption caused by a major security flaw, Andy Burnham said "unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common".
The government has drawn up recommendations for households to have three days' worth of bottled water and tinned food to deal with a crisis such as a war, an online attack or a natural disaster.
Burnham added: "It's not about panicking... It's about just taking sensible measures to have enough in the house to tide you over should there be a difficult situation."
At Labour's conference last month, Housing Secretary Angela Raynerjoked that her emergency box,externalwould include a bottle of wine.
She said she'd include: "Mascara, concealer, I don't know, a bottle of Sauvignon Blanc, a tin of baked beans because you've gotta have some baked beans, and I like a good tin of custard as well so I think that'll keep me going for a while."
Asked whether he agreed with her, Burnham told BBC Radio 5 Live's Matt Chorley: "Well, I'm not sure a bottle of wine is your best first port of call if you're in a slightly crisis situation, but it probably helps when you've done the hard work.
"But I'll stick to the basics I think - I do like my beans, so I have plenty of those in the cupboard, and soup.
"I think those are the kind of things that I would recommend people to have, as well as Twiglets, I'm not sure I can get by for too long without those."
Last month, theNational Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at riskgiven the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis and said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.
The chief executive of the Cold Chain Federation, which represents firms transporting temperature-controlled foods, also told the BBC the UK is being targeted by Russian cyber-hackers who "know that there are pinch points in the food supply system".
Speaking at a wildfire resilience summit in Liverpool, Burnham denied the government had failed to properly prepare, saying: "No, we're having the conversation with people about being better prepared because we're living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common.
"Obviously, weather events, and we're in a situation today where the UK is facing storms and obviously, we feel for the people without power in Cornwall right now.
"It is just having those supplies in the house to get you through those moments. So we are having that conversation about resilience."
Why should I stockpile and what will I need?
Military aircraft to help get UK 'on front foot' to fight wildfires, Burnham says
Prepare for supply chain disruption from cyber or climate emergencies, Streeting warns
A checklist drawn up by the government recommends having nine litres of water per person – enough for three days – along with non-perishable food such as tinned meat and vegetables or dried fruit.
The government suggests having an FM radio, either battery or wind-up. During a national crisis, the BBC would prioritise broadcasting news, as well as health and safety information. In the event of a severe power cut, FM radio will be the best way to receive these updates.
The list also suggests hand sanitiser, wet wipes and toiletries, food for any pets, supplies for any babies, a torch, blankets, a charged power bank for devices, cash in case payment systems collapse, a first aid kit and copies of important documents.
Earlier, Treasury minister James Murray told BBC Breakfast he has not yet followed the government's guidance on stockpiling supplies to prepare for a crisis.
He said he had a stockpile of coffee, but pointed out that neighbouring countries including Ireland, France and the Netherlands had given the same guidance "for quite a long time".
He added: "I'm not going to pretend I've followed all that advice myself yet."
Speaking on the same programme, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said she was "stocked up for the week at any time".
She said the previous Conservative government had issued similar advice on preparing for emergencies, but added: "What I'm more concerned about is that it doesn't look like [the government] are explaining what the risks we are under are, and what they are doing about the big things.
"Families can stock up but what's going on with defence, the cyber attacks, the hybrid warfare? The money to look after the country has not been forthcoming."

title: Ex-Tory campaign chief and his wife receive suspended sentences over election bets
summary: Anthony Lee passed confidential information to his wife Laura Lee about when the 2024 general election would be held.
body:
Anthony Lee and his wife Laura pleaded guilty at Southwark Crown Court on Thursday
The Conservatives' former director of campaigning and his wife have received suspended prison sentences after they admitted to cheating at gambling by placing bets on the date of the 2024 general election.
Anthony Lee used "inside information" emerging from a private meeting called by then-Prime Minister Rishi Sunak to bet on the general election date months before it took place, Southwark Crown Court heard.
Lee and his wife Laura stood to win more than £23,000 had their cheating not been uncovered, the court heard.
Lee was sentenced to 10 months and two weeks' imprisonment, suspended for 12 months, while his wife was sentenced to four months and two weeks' imprisonment, suspended for a year.
Amy Hind, a former Tory party employee who was working as an NHS business support manager, was also sentenced to six months' imprisonment, suspended for a year, after previously pleading guilty to cheating on the date of the election.
Judge Tony Baumgartner, sentencing the three of them, said their conduct "risked undermining" the confidence the public has in the Conservative Party "as an institution", "undermining trust in the democratic process" and the "integrity of the gambling system".
The trio were among several people charged with betting offences by the Gambling Commission.
The trials of other defendants will take place next year and in 2028.
Former Conservative MP Craig Williams, who was Sunak's closest parliamentary aide at the time,pleaded guilty in Juneand will be sentenced at a later date.
Sunak's decision to call a general election for July 2024 was a surprise to many, including several Conservative MPs, who were expecting an autumn date.
The court heard that Sunak held a private Downing Street meeting on 10 March of that year to discuss possible dates.
Neither Lee nor his wife attended the meeting, but the couple began betting online on the election being held in July or between July and September, the court heard.
Prosecutor Zoe Johnson said: "Although not at Number 10, the overwhelming inference is that Anthony Lee was receiving inside information as the meeting went on and was acting upon it."
She added: "Together they were using it to make a profit for themselves."
Lee placed or tried to place 71 bets during the period, while his wife placed eight and attempted a ninth, the court heard.
Baumgartner described Anthony Lee as a "central figure" in the preparation of the general election, who sat at a group of desks within Tory HQ known as the "God Pod".
Representing Lee, barrister Richard Pratt said his client did not concretely know the working date of the election, saying it "still represented a gamble from his point of view".
The barrister told the court: "It was always possible the prime minister could change his mind."
Pratt said there "wasn't any direct manipulation" by the defendant.
Laura Lee worked for the Tories as their "head of international" and had been selected as the party candidate for Bristol North West for the election.
Baumgartner said she had no involvement in the election planning and her access to information "came predominantly" from her husband.
The court heard Hind's husband Anthony worked as a deputy digital director for the Conservatives but did not place any bets himself.
Baumgartner said Hind's husband "was party to emails relating to the forthcoming general election and was one potential source of your inside information".
The judge later said "someone else who worked within the heart of CCHQ" could have given her the "highly confidential" information.
The court heard Hind placed four bets and made three further unsuccessful attempts to place bets. The unsuccessful attempts were for £767, £700 and £750.
The judge described Hind's bets as a "clear departure from your previous betting history", noting: "Before the present offending, your largest stake had been £10.50, and only seven of your 3,399 recorded selections involved a stake of that amount."
Neither of the defendants have previous convictions and they are all of good previous character, the court heard.
Baumgartner described them all as having expressed remorse for their actions.
The trio are now subject to a 12-month prohibited activity requirement, banning them from accessing or using online gambling websites or applications.
Anthony Lee was ordered to complete 100 hours of unpaid work and pay more than £6,600 in compensation to a betting company, while Laura Lee must carry out 40 hours of unpaid work and pay £4,265.
Hind was ordered to complete 50 hours of unpaid work.
Katharine Diamond, General Counsel of regulators the Gambling Commission, reacted to the sentencing of the trio by saying "justice has been served".
She described the case as "a first of its kind" and said it demonstrated the commission's "commitment to protecting the integrity of betting markets".

title: Trump says Burnham 'getting it done' after Jackdaw decision
summary: The US president has praised Burnham after the government allowed gas drilling in the North Sea's Jackdaw field.
body:
Donald Trump said Andy Burnham's decision on Jackdaw would "make the UK a very rich country"
US President Donald Trump has praised Prime Minister Andy Burnham for the UK government's decision to approve production from the North Sea's Jackdaw gas field.
He said he had spoken with Burnham, telling reporters on Friday that the decision would "make the UK a very rich country".
Trump said: "The other prime minister, the previous man, Starmer. He's a very nice man, but he never got it done, and this one is getting it."
The decision had been subject to intense debate around its environment and economic impact and came after years of legal challenges.
The Jackdaw platform is located east of Aberdeen
Burnham announced the decision to approve the drilling of the Jackdaw gas field earlier this week.
Jackdaw is situated 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.
Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund.
Environmental campaigners say the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.
Based on official forecasts for the amount of gas the UK will need over the next decade, that suggests Jackdaw has the potential to meet around 1.6% of total projected national gas demand between 2026 and 2036.
Operators say it could be connected to the Great British gas network within weeks and could produce gas for the next 11 years.
Trump responded to the decision on Friday, but appeared to confuse oil and gas.
He said: "They're opening up the North Sea oil. I've been after them to do that for two years."
Trump added: "Andy is getting it done, and I guess it's against the liberal principle, but he knows what's right. It's going to make UK a very wealthy country."
In a discussion on Friday, Burnham and Trump spoke about the decision to approve Jackdaw.
The two leaders "agreed on the significant benefits this will bring to the UK, boosting the economy and supporting jobs for British workers", a statement from Number 10 read.
It added that Trump and Burnham "welcomed the continued collaboration between UK and US companies, especially on nuclear power".
Earlier this week, on Wednesday, Trump said the decision was "great news for the wealth and prosperity" of the UK.
Writing on his Truth Social platform, Trump urged the UK to go "full blast" and called the North Sea "one of the greatest and most prosperous areas of oil in the world".
A decision is yet to be takenon whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the prime minister of "dithering" on Jackdaw and said a ban on new oil and gas licences should be repealed.
However, Burnham said her party had "messed up" the original decision by not giving any regard to climate obligations - things he said "have to be considered in the round".
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said gas from Jackdaw would be in homes and businesses this month, but that it would not lower energy bills this winter.
She said the decision was "compatible" with legally binding climate commitments, adding:  "We remain resolute in ending new licences for oil and gas and achieving net zero by 2050."
Environmental groups have criticised the Jackdaw approval. Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said it was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change.
Meanwhile, Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments".
During their Friday talks, Trump and Burnham spoke about the Falkland Islands and the Sea Lion oilfield project, a joint venture between British and Israeli companies.
In September, the Argentinian government threatened to impose economic sanctions on firms exploiting oil close to the Falkland Islands, and earlier this month, itbegan legal action to stop the exploration of oil and gas fields.
Burnham raised the "economic consequences ofArgentina's coercive measures for the UK and USand reiterated the importance of respecting the Islanders' right to develop their natural resources", Downing Street said.
The two leaders also discussed Ukraine, with the prime minister underlining the importance for Ukraine "to have full access to Starlink so they can continue to defend themselves against Russia's full-scale invasion", according to Number 10.
Starlink technology is a satellite system owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company which Ukraine has relied upon during the war.
In recent days,Ukraine has been recording issues with the network, according to sources within the defence ministry. This has affected the country's ability to use attack drones and co-ordinate defensive operations.
The Downing Street statement added: "The Prime Minister recognised the work of President Trump to bring Putin to the negotiation table and the leaders agreed to work together, alongside international partners to bring an end to the bloodshed."

title: Green councillors face Labour deadline to disown Zionism policy
summary: Green leaders have been given until Sunday to disown their party's "Zionism is racism" conference vote.
body:
Green leader Zack Polanski has faced criticism over his response to the Zionism motion
Labour is set to decide whether to end power-sharing with Green councillors after demanding they disown their party's policy that Zionism is a form of racism.
The BBC has been told Green groups have been given until Sunday to respond to the demand, after which Labour's ruling National Executive Committee (NEC) will decide whether the party will continue with local deals to share power.
Green groups in some areas have publicly stated they do not agree with the policy or have distanced themselves from it, reducing the likelihood the pacts will end.
But in other areas Green councillors are yet to specify where they stand on the issue, meaning local alliances appear more vulnerable to collapse.
The issue is the most acute in nine local authorities where Greens are key partners in power-sharing arrangements, such as making up majorities that enable budgets to be passed and policy decisions to be made.
These include Sheffield City Council, Warwick District Council and Lewes District Council, three authorities where Labour and the Greens are in direct coalition.
The other areas where the Greens play a key role are: West Oxfordshire District Council, Stafford Borough Council, Havant Borough Council, Broadland District Council, Derbyshire Dales District Council and Wealden District Council.
In other areas, Green councillors are not central to local alliances continuing to function. These include Runnymede Borough Council, where Green councillors have left the local ruling alliance folllowing Labour's ultimatum.
In some areas, such as Lewes, Wealden, Broadland, West Sussex and North Somerset, local Green groups have distanced themselves from their party's Zionism policy, or said they do not agree with it.
But other Green groups are yet to publicly respond to Labour's demands, meaning there is greater uncertainty over the future of their co-operation with the party.
In Stafford, the power-sharing arrangement means the Greens have one cabinet member on the authority, councillor Tony Pearce, who holds the climate change portfolio.
Councillor Pearce has been contacted for comment but has not yet responded.
The leader of the Stafford Green group, Doug Rouxel told the BBC they were "formulating a response" to Labour's letter which they would like to put to party members first.
Labour confirmed the if the Greens refused to reject the Zionism policy, a process would then be triggered to remove Pearce from his cabinet position in Stafford.
Elsewhere, the leader of the Labour group on the Green-led Lewes District Council has resigned from the party, following his own party's ultimatum.
Chris Collier, who has been contacted for comment, will now sit as an independent cabinet member on the Labour-Green alliance that was formed to run the council in May 2023.
The BBC has been told Collier did not agree with the tone of Labour's ultimatum to the Green Party over the Zionism policy.
The "Zionism is racism" motion was passed by members of the Green Party of England and Wales at its annual conference in Brighton last month.
The policy motion adopted by members said Zionism was an ideology that supported an "ethnonationalist Jewish state" that had led to the "disenfranchisement and destruction" of Palestinians.
It backed the creation of a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.
It has led to a backlash from Jewish groups, as well as criticism from senior Green figures, including four of its five MPs.
Green leader Zack Polanski, who skipped the conference vote to unsuccessfully campaign for election in a Westminster by-election, has said he wants to see the "imperfect" motion amended in future.
Labour councillors require the approval of the party's NEC before entering into local tie-ups.
According to the party's rulebook, local groups must also "stand down" from power-sharing arrangements when asked to do so by their regional office.
By contrast, the Green Party of England and Wales allows local groups to make the final decision on where and whether to share power locally.
A Green Party spokesperson said: "For the Labour government to conflate criticism of Israel with antisemitism is disappointing and wrong.
"Trying to tell local parties what to do and who they can work with is undemocratic."

title: Chancellor says he will cut 'pointless paperwork' to save businesses up to £800m
summary: Ministers say the changes in regulations will reduce unnecessary bureaucracy.
body:
John Healey becomes the latest chancellor to pledge to cut red tape for businesses ahead of his first Budget
The chancellor has announced plans to slash "form-filling and pointless paperwork" to save UK businesses up to £800m.
Ministers have said the proposed changes in regulations, announced ahead of John Healey's first Budget on Wednesday, will reduce unnecessary bureaucracy for businesses.
The move is part of a broader effort in the Budget to offer households and businesses more support amid rising costs.
In response to the announcement, the Conservatives said Labour had only made problems worse for businesses.
"Labour have finally admitted that endless red tape is hammering businesses and killing jobs across the country," shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said.
Healey acknowledged British firms are "fed up with form-filling and pointless paperwork" eating into time and money that would be more valuable invested into their businesses.
He becomes the latest chancellor to pledge to slash red tape, which he said will allow businesses more "breathing space" to invest and create good jobs.
The changes should make compliance guidance easier, and simplify the reporting rules firms have to follow, the Treasury said.
Ministers have claimed this will save almost £800m in administrative and tariff costs.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Healey are expected to meet some business leaders on Friday at No 10 North.
Burnham said that it's unfair "pointless bureaucracy gets in the way" of hard-working people building their businesses.
"If you run a business, you want to spend your time serving your customers, creating jobs and growing your firm, not filling in unnecessary forms," Burnham said.
The government has set itself a target of cutting regulation by 25% by the end of the current Parliament.
The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) Chief Executive Rain Newton Smith has welcomed the plans, but said the test would be in delivering reform.
Meanwhile, the shadow chancellor argued that the employment act had only made "the situation worse and has created a youth jobs emergency".
"John Healey must get a grip in his Budget next week. He must back our Conservative plans to cut welfare and cut taxes so we can get Britain working again," he said.
